extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for novelists writing historical fiction on how to research, incorporate period detail, balance authenticity with storytelling, and handle sources (especially the internet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance authenticity and storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: There’s a funny sort of tension that occurs when writing historical fiction: Is it possible to achieve total historical accuracy while still telling a great story? ... these are some lessons I’ve learned, in that balance of authenticity and accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slavish literalism that makes prose pedantic or unintelligible to modern readers (e.g., reproducing archaic words that modern readers won't understand). Also avoid strictly making characters typical of their station/gender if that would make them unable to drive the plot—allow room to adapt historical behavior for compelling character action. Use informed choices to preserve readability and narrative energy while remaining grounded in period reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have fun with the research, but do your homework
rubrics_metrics.description: Have fun with the research, but do your homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect good reference books and become comfortable with your chosen time period. Learn both the large-scale historical context and the details of daily life so the setting feels authentic. Research should inform the backdrop without overwhelming the story; thorough homework produces believable details that support the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the characters engage with the historical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the characters engage with the historical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than dumping facts on the reader, show historical detail through characters' sensory experiences and interactions: sight, smell, touch, sound (e.g., offal on cobblestones, tallow candles' light, feeling a leech on skin). Use 'show, don't tell' to integrate facts naturally into scenes so the setting feels lived-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow characters to question and explore their place in society
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow your characters to question and explore their place in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters' perspectives and inquiries to reveal political, social, and cultural context. Ask what expectations existed for different groups (women, sailors, criminals) and how people from different social positions interacted—letting characters probe those norms communicates historical context organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the internet wisely, to inspire and inform
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the internet wisely, to inspire and inform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat online resources as valuable tools for practical questions and sensory/visual research—interactive maps, videos (e.g., interior tours), images, and digitized historical documents can answer logistics (distances, layouts) and evoke atmospherics. Use tools like walking directions and tourist videos to supplement primary/secondary sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that the internet can be bad for historical research
rubrics_metrics.description: The internet can be bad, bad, bad for historical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The web contains flawed information, plagiarized material, half-truths, and outright lies. Use sources cautiously (the author specifically warns about Wikipedia). Verify facts against at least two independent sources when possible; identical wording across sites may indicate copying rather than verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t fret the details; let the story be told
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t fret the details; let the story be told.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for accuracy but accept that some things will require an informed guess. Prioritize story and readability; if you fudge an element for narrative reasons, be transparent about it (for example, in a historical note at the end). Avoid paralysis over minor uncertainties that would stall the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love the process and accept that readers will find errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Love the process, because readers will still find errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with careful checking, copyediting, and proofreading, mistakes will slip through (timeline, geography, small inconsistencies). Be prepared to receive correction gracefully: thank readers, laugh, and move on rather than obsessing. Practical implication: focus editorial effort where it most benefits story and clarity.
